title: Testing and Evaluation of Health Care Applications of Large Language Models: A Systematic Review
authors: Bedi S et al. (last: Shah NH)
metadata_verified_via: NSF PAR record + news page (reused 2026-11-23); PMC11480901 blocked by captcha 2026-11-27
objective: Characterise how health-care LLM applications are tested and evaluated
dataset_sample: 519 studies
metrics: Share of studies by data type, task, evaluation dimension
main_findings: 5% used real patient care data; medical knowledge tasks 44.5%, diagnosis 19.5%; QA 84.2% of NLP tasks, dialogue 3.3%; accuracy primary dimension in 95.4%; fairness/bias/toxicity 15.8%; deployment 4.6%; calibration/uncertainty 1.2%
limitations: Full text not read; review window ends Feb 2024 (before most agentic CDS work)
relevance: P4/RQ1: evaluation dominated by exam accuracy; uncertainty rarely measured
supports_or_contradicts: Supports need for safety/abstention metrics and real-data evaluation; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Exam-QA accuracy dominates; calibration/uncertainty measured in 1.2% of studies

title: A framework for human evaluation of large language models in healthcare derived from literature review
authors: Tam TYC et al. (15 authors; last: Wang Y)
objective: Review human evaluation practice for healthcare LLMs and propose a framework
dataset_sample: 142 studies
metrics: QUEST principles: Quality of information; Understanding and reasoning; Expression style and persona; Safety and harm; Trust and confidence
main_findings: Proposes QUEST (5 principles, 3 phases: planning; implementation and adjudication; scoring and review); reports gaps in reliability, generalizability and applicability of human evaluation
limitations: Full text not read; evaluator counts/blinding statistics not extracted
relevance: RQ1/RQ2: design of expert review subset (safety and harm; trust)
supports_or_contradicts: Supports safety-centred human evaluation
claims_supported: Human evaluation of health LLMs is non-standardised; safety and harm is a core principle

title: Holistic evaluation of large language models for medical tasks with MedHELM
authors: Bedi S, Cui H, Fuentes M, et al. (last: Shah NH)
published_version_checked: yes: arXiv 2505.23802 (2025) published in Nature Medicine 2026 (PMID 41559415); volume/pages not seen
metadata_verified_via: Stanford Health Care publication record (2026-11-27); arXiv abstract (reused)
objective: Holistic, clinician-validated evaluation of LLMs on real medical tasks
architecture_methods: Taxonomy of 5 categories, 22 subcategories, 121 tasks; LLM-jury evaluation; cost estimation
models_tools: 9 frontier LLMs incl. DeepSeek R1, o3-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet
dataset_sample: Journal: 37 evaluations; arXiv v2: 35 benchmarks (17 existing, 18 new). Access/licence per benchmark not verified (mix of public, gated and private)
metrics: Win rate; normalized accuracy per category; LLM-jury vs clinician ICC; estimated cost
main_findings: Journal abstract: reasoning models (DeepSeek R1, o3-mini) 66% win rate; Claude 3.5 Sonnet comparable at 15% lower computational cost. arXiv v2: CDS normalized accuracy 0.56-0.72 (second-lowest category); jury-clinician ICC 0.47 vs clinician-clinician 0.43, ROUGE-L 0.36, BERTScore-F1 0.44; Claude 3.5 Sonnet ~40% lower estimated cost
limitations: Preprint and journal numbers differ (35 vs 37 benchmarks; ~40% vs 15% cost); jury agreement moderate; cost estimated
relevance: P4/RQ4: cost reporting precedent; RQ1: CDS among weakest categories
supports_or_contradicts: Supports holistic, cost-aware evaluation; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: CDS is a weak category for frontier LLMs; cost should be reported with performance

title: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health
authors: Arora RK et al. (last: Singhal K), OpenAI
published_version_checked: no journal version found in this pass
metadata_verified_via: arXiv abstract + HTML (reused); GitHub openai/simple-evals for licence (2026-11-27)
objective: Rubric-based evaluation of LLMs in realistic health conversations
architecture_methods: Physician-written conversation-specific rubrics; model-based grading; negative criteria subtract points
dataset_sample: 5,000 multi-turn conversations, mostly synthetically generated; 262 physicians; 48,562 unique rubric criteria; themes incl. responding under uncertainty 21.4%, context seeking 11.9%, emergency referrals 9.6%. Licence: reference implementation in openai/simple-evals, MIT licence; repo not updated for new models since July 2025
metrics: Rubric score; axes completeness 39%, accuracy 33%, context awareness 16%, communication 8%, instruction following 4%
main_findings: GPT-3.5 Turbo 16%, GPT-4o 32%, o3 60%; top HealthBench Hard 32%; GPT-4.1 nano beat GPT-4o at ~25x lower cost
limitations: Mostly synthetic conversations; model-graded; industry-produced; Consensus subset high precision/lower recall
relevance: RQ1/P2: themes map to ESCALATE_NOW, NEED_MORE_INFO, caveats/abstain; candidate secondary test set
supports_or_contradicts: Supports status-level behaviours as evaluation targets
claims_supported: Emergency referral, context seeking and uncertainty are recognised evaluation themes

title: An evaluation framework for clinical use of large language models in patient interaction tasks
authors: Johri S et al. (last: Rajpurkar P)
objective: Evaluate LLM clinical accuracy in conversational patient-interaction formats
architecture_methods: Clinical LLM converses with patient-AI; grader-AI (GPT-4) scores; dermatologist review of 180 conversations
dataset_sample: 2,000 vignettes: 1,800 MedQA-USMLE (12 specialties), 100 Derm-Public, 100 Derm-Private; 5 runs -> 10,000 conversations. Release/licence not verified
metrics: Diagnostic accuracy (MCQ and free response) by format; history-taking completeness; grader-expert agreement
main_findings: GPT-4 MCQ vignette 0.820 -> multi-turn 0.627; FRQ 0.486 -> 0.264; GPT-4 complete history in 71.11% of conversations; grader-expert agreement 93.35%
limitations: Patient-AI limits; expert review only in dermatology; only 7B open models
relevance: P1/RQ1: accuracy drops in interactive format; supports open/closed option design
supports_or_contradicts: Supports realistic, interactive evaluation
claims_supported: MCQ accuracy overstates conversational performance

title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
authors: Hager P, Jungmann F, Holland R, et al. (last: Braren R)
objective: Evaluate LLMs on autonomous clinical decision-making with real EHR data
architecture_methods: LLM requests exam/labs/imaging via action fields then diagnoses and plans treatment; information-order and amount experiments
models_tools: Llama 2 Chat, OASST, WizardLM (70B); 4 hospitalists reader study (80 patients)
dataset_sample: MIMIC-IV-Ext-CDM: 2,400 real MIMIC-IV ED patients with abdominal pain (appendicitis 957, cholecystitis 648, pancreatitis 538, diverticulitis 257). Access: PhysioNet credentialed, PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data License 1.5.0, DUA 1.5.0, CITI Data or Specimens Only Research
metrics: Diagnostic accuracy; guideline adherence; info-request behaviour; formatting/tool hallucination frequency; order sensitivity
main_findings: Models 16-25 points below physicians (P<0.001); autonomous accuracy 45.5%, 54.9%, 53.9%; tool hallucination every 2-5 patients; info order changed accuracy by up to 18.0 points; GPT-4 not testable under MIMIC agreements at the time
limitations: 4 pathologies, 1 complaint; US/English; small reader study; only open 70B models
relevance: P1/RQ1/RQ3: real-data testbed with closed diagnosis set; order sensitivity
supports_or_contradicts: Supports P1; motivates deterministic validation
claims_supported: LLMs underperform physicians on real-EHR decisions; order sensitivity up to 18 points

authors: Li SS, Balachandran V, Feng S, Ilgen JS, Pierson E, Koh PW, Tsvetkov Y

authors: Khandekar N, Jin Q, Xiong G, Dunn S, Applebaum SS, Anwar Z, Sarfo-Gyamfi M, Safranek CW, Anwar AA, Zhang A, Gilson A, Singer MB, Dave A, Taylor A, Zhang A, Chen Q, Lu Z

title: First, do NOHARM: a medical safety benchmark and randomized study of physician and AI teaming on clinical consultations
authors: Wu D et al. (57 authors; last: Goh E)
published_version_checked: no journal reference on arXiv page (2026-11-27)
objective: Measure clinical safety (harm) of LLM recommendations and physician-AI teaming

models_tools: 20 LLMs and 4 RAG clinical AI tools; multi-agent teaming variant
dataset_sample: 1,100 primary care-to-specialist consultation cases, 10 specialties, 4,249 management options, 12,747 expert annotations; public benchmark and leaderboard (licence not verified); case origin not stated in abstract
metrics: Severe harm rate per case; share of severe errors that are omissions
baselines: Generalist LLMs vs clinical RAG tools vs multi-agent teaming; physicians with vs without AI
main_findings: Severe harm potential in up to 24.6% of cases; errors of omission >80% of severe errors; clinical AI tools outperform generalist LLMs; multi-agent teaming further improved generalist models; RCT n=101 physicians: AI assistance improved performance but physicians omitted valuable AI recommendations

title: How well do LLMs cite relevant medical references? An evaluation framework and analyses
authors: Wu K, Wu E, Casasola A, Zhang A, Wei K, Nguyen T, Riantawan S, Shi P, Ho D, Zou J
published_version_checked: published version exists as PMC12003634 titled 'An Automated Framework for Assessing How Well LLMs Cite Relevant Medical References'; journal not confirmed (captcha)
metadata_verified_via: arXiv HTML v1; Stanford Law publication listing
objective: Measure whether LLM-cited sources support medical statements
architecture_methods: SourceCheckup: GPT-4 question generation, statement parsing, URL fetching, statement-source pairwise support judgement
models_tools: GPT-4 (RAG, Bing), GPT-4 API, Claude v2.1, Mistral Medium, Gemini Pro
dataset_sample: 1,200 questions (400 each MayoClinic, UpToDate, Reddit r/AskDocs); >40,000 statement-source pairs; 284 clinician-annotated pairs; authors state questions and annotations are open-sourced (repository/licence not seen)
metrics: URL validity; statement-level support; response-level support
main_findings: GPT-4 (RAG): URL validity 99.2%, statement support 69.4%, response support 54.3%; GPT-4 API 69.2/42.2/22.7%; Claude v2.1 62.1/25.2/13.7%; Gemini Pro 41.3/14.3/7.6%; auto-judge vs doctor consensus 88.0% (N=284) vs inter-doctor 85.2% (p=0.21)

title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations
authors: Gao T, Yen H, Yu J, Chen D
objective: Benchmark and metrics for citation quality in LLM generation
architecture_methods: NLI-based (TRUE, T5-11B) citation recall and precision
dataset_sample: ASQA, QAMPARI (Wikipedia 21M passages), ELI5 (Sphere 899M passages); general domain, not medical
metrics: Citation recall: statement has >=1 citation and concatenated citations entail it; citation precision: citation scores 1 if its statement has recall 1 and the citation is not irrelevant (irrelevant = does not entail alone and others still entail)
main_findings: On ELI5 best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time; human-auto kappa 0.698 (recall), 0.525 (precision); auto accuracy vs human 85.1% (recall), 77.6% (precision)
limitations: General domain; partial support not handled
relevance: P3/RQ2: formal definitions for citation precision/recall
supports_or_contradicts: Supports P3
claims_supported: Standard definitions for citation recall/precision
